units.title: 拼音 Pinyin: letters and initials

lessons.title: 1. What pinyin is
lessons.subtitle: Syllables, initials, finals and tones

explanations.title: Writing the sound of Chinese
explanations.body: Chinese is written with characters. A character shows a meaning, but it does not show how to say it. Pinyin is the system of Latin letters that writes the sounds of Mandarin. Dictionaries, textbooks and phone keyboards all use it, so it is the way into the spoken language. Pinyin letters do not always sound the way they do in English: x, q, c, z, zh and ü are the usual surprises, and the next lessons take them one group at a time. You do not need to learn the characters in these first lessons. They are there so you can hear real words.

examples.text: 你好
examples.translation: nǐ hǎo — hello

examples.text: 谢谢
examples.translation: xiè xie — thank you

examples.text: 再见
examples.translation: zài jiàn — goodbye

explanations.title: Every syllable has three parts
explanations.body: A Mandarin syllable is one unit of sound, and each Chinese character is read as one syllable. A syllable has an initial, a final and a tone. The initial is the consonant at the start. The final is everything after it: a vowel, or a vowel plus n or ng. A few syllables have no initial and begin with the final. Mandarin has 21 initials, 36 finals and four tones, plus a light neutral tone.

options: A second set of Chinese characters
A way of writing the sounds of Chinese with Latin letters
A spelling system for English words
exercises.explanation: Pinyin spells how Mandarin sounds. It is not a dialect and it is not a kind of character.

exercises.prompt: How many tones does Mandarin have, not counting the neutral tone?
exercises.explanation: There are four tones, plus a light neutral tone.

exercises.prompt: What are the three parts of a Mandarin syllable?
exercises.explanation: Every syllable is an initial (sometimes missing), a final and a tone.

exercises.prompt: In kàn, what is the initial?
exercises.explanation: The initial is the consonant at the start: k. The final is an.

exercises.prompt: In kàn, what is the final?
exercises.explanation: The final is everything after the initial: an.

exercises.prompt: In zhōng, what is the initial?
exercises.explanation: Zh is a single initial, not z followed by h.
ài starts straight with the final ai. The others begin with m, sh and h.

exercises.prompt: Which statement about pinyin letters is true?
options: Some letters, such as x, q and c, sound different from English
Pinyin uses a different alphabet from Latin letters
Every letter sounds just like its English twin
exercises.explanation: Learn the pinyin value of each letter. Do not assume the English one.

exercises.prompt: What does the tone of a syllable do?
options: It helps decide the meaning of the word
It shows where the word ends
Nothing: it is only for singing
exercises.explanation: Syllables spelled the same but said with different tones are different words, as the tones lesson shows.

exercises.prompt: A Chinese character is normally read as how many syllables?
options: As many as it has strokes

lessons.title: 2. b, p, m, f
lessons.subtitle: The first four initials, and the puff of air

explanations.title: Four lip sounds
explanations.body: B and p are made with both lips, m is the same sound as in English, and f is made with the top teeth on the lower lip. The difference between b and p is not voicing but a puff of air. P is aspirated: say it with a strong puff, like the p in “pie”. B has no puff and sounds closer to the p in “spy”. Hold a thin strip of paper in front of your mouth: it should flutter for p and stay still for b.

rows: like the p in “spy”: no puff
like the p in “pie”: strong puff

explanations.title: Puff or no puff
explanations.body: English speakers tend to hear b and p as the same sound. In Mandarin they are different letters, so they make different words. Listen for the puff, not for any buzzing.

exercises.prompt: Which initial is said with a strong puff of air?
exercises.explanation: P is aspirated. B is not.

exercises.prompt: Which initial is made with the top teeth on the lower lip?

exercises.explanation: 爸 is read bà and means “dad”.
怕 is read pà and means “afraid”.
妈 is read mā and means “mum”.
笔 is read bǐ and means “a pen”.
皮 is read pí and means “skin, leather”.

exercises.prompt: To check you are saying p and not b, a paper strip held before your mouth should…
exercises.explanation: The puff of air is what moves the paper: it is there for p and absent for b.
Both are tone 1 with the final a. Only the initial changes.

lessons.title: 3. d, t, n, l
lessons.subtitle: Tongue-tip sounds, and n or l before ü

explanations.title: Four tongue-tip sounds
explanations.body: Put the tip of your tongue on the ridge just behind your top teeth. D and t work like b and p: t has a strong puff of air and d has none (like the t in “sty”). N and l are as in English. After n and l the vowel ü keeps its two dots: nǚ and lǜ. (After j, q and x the dots are dropped. A later lesson explains why.)

rows: like the t in “sty”: no puff
like the t in “tie”: strong puff

explanations.title: Pairs to listen for
explanations.body: As with b and p, the puff makes the difference. N and l are harder for some learners: n sends air through the nose, l lets it flow around the sides of the tongue.

exercises.prompt: Which initial has a strong puff of air?
exercises.explanation: T is aspirated. D is not.
大 is read dà and means “big”.
他 is read tā and means “he”.
那 is read nà and means “that”.
拉 is read lā and means “to pull”.
女 is read nǚ and means “woman”.
绿 is read lǜ and means “green”.

exercises.prompt: Which pair differs only by a puff of air?
exercises.explanation: D and t are the unaspirated and aspirated pair. N and l differ in another way.

exercises.prompt: What happens to the dots of ü after n and l?
exercises.explanation: After n and l you must keep the dots, because nu and nü are different syllables.

lessons.title: 4. g, k, h
lessons.subtitle: Throat sounds

explanations.title: Three back-of-the-mouth sounds
explanations.body: G and k are made at the back of the tongue, and follow the same rule as b/p and d/t: k has a strong puff of air, g has none (like the k in “sky”). H is like English h, but rougher, made further back in the throat, a little like the ch in Scottish “loch”. These three go only with a, e, u and the finals built on them.

rows: like the k in “sky”: no puff
like the k in “key”: strong puff
a rough h, from the throat

explanations.title: More examples
explanations.body: The same three letters with other finals. Notice how the sound of the initial stays the same while the rest of the syllable changes.

exercises.prompt: Which initial has a strong puff of air?
exercises.explanation: K is aspirated. G is not.

exercises.prompt: Which sound is described as a rough h from the throat?
exercises.explanation: H is made further back than English h.
哥 is read gē and means “older brother”.
课 is read kè and means “a lesson”.
河 is read hé and means “a river”.
开 is read kāi and means “to open”.
好 is read hǎo and means “good”.
喝 is read hē and means “to drink”.

exercises.prompt: gǔ, kǔ and hú differ in…
options: the initial (and, for hu, the tone)
nothing: they are the same word
exercises.explanation: G, k and h make three different syllables.

lessons.title: 5. j, q, x
lessons.subtitle: Palatal sounds: tongue tip down

explanations.title: Tongue tip behind the lower teeth
explanations.body: For j, q and x rest the tip of your tongue against the back of your lower front teeth, and spread your lips as if smiling. In English, j, ch and sh are usually made with the tongue tip near the ridge behind the top teeth. In these three sounds it never goes there. Q is aspirated (a strong puff of air) and j is not, just as with b and p.

rows: like the j in “jeep”, tongue tip down: no puff
like the ch in “cheese”, tongue tip down: strong puff
like the sh in “she”, tongue tip down

explanations.title: J, q and x take only i and ü
explanations.body: These three initials are only ever followed by i, by ü, or by a final that begins with i or ü. When the vowel is ü the two dots are not written, so ü looks like u: ju, qu, xu. So there is no syllable ja, qa or xo in Mandarin.

exercises.prompt: Where should the tongue tip be for j, q and x?
options: Curled back toward the roof of the mouth
Against the back of the lower front teeth
Against the ridge behind the top teeth
exercises.explanation: In j, q and x the tip stays down. That is what separates them from zh, ch and sh.

exercises.prompt: Which of j, q and x has a strong puff of air?

exercises.explanation: 鸡 is read jī and means “chicken”.
七 is read qī and means “seven”.
西 is read xī and means “west”.
去 is read qù and means “to go”.
句 is read jù and means “a sentence”.
千 is read qiān and means “a thousand”.

exercises.prompt: In qù, the u is really…
exercises.explanation: After j, q and x the letter written u is the vowel ü: ju, qu, xu.

lessons.title: 6. z, c, s
lessons.subtitle: Tongue tip on the teeth

explanations.title: Three sounds made at the teeth
explanations.body: Z, c and s are made with the tip of the tongue just behind the top front teeth. S is as in English. Z is not the English z: it is a d and an s said together, like the ds in “buds” at the start of a syllable. C is a t and an s said together, like the ts in “cats”, with a strong puff of air.

rows: like the ds in “buds”: no puff
like the ts in “cats”: strong puff

explanations.title: The buzzing i
explanations.body: After z, c and s the letter i does not sound like “ee”. It is a buzz made in the same tongue position, with the tongue where it already is. So zì, cì and sì end in a buzz, not in a vowel you can say separately.

exercises.prompt: Which initial sounds like the ds in “buds”?
exercises.explanation: Z is a d and s together. It is not the English z.

exercises.prompt: Which initial sounds like the ts in “cats”, with a puff?
exercises.explanation: C is a t and s together with a strong puff.
在 is read zài and means “to be at”.
菜 is read cài and means “a dish, vegetables”.
三 is read sān and means “three”.
字 is read zì and means “a character”.
四 is read sì and means “four”.
错 is read cuò and means “wrong”.

exercises.prompt: How is the i in sì pronounced?
options: A buzz in the same tongue position as the s
exercises.explanation: After z, c and s the i is a buzz, not a separate vowel.

lessons.title: 7. zh, ch, sh, r
lessons.subtitle: Curling the tongue back

explanations.title: Tongue tip curled back
explanations.body: Curl the tip of your tongue up and back toward the roof of your mouth, without touching it. Zh is like the j in “judge”, ch is like the ch in “church” with a strong puff, and sh is like the sh in “shoe”, all with the tongue curled. R is a buzzing sound between English r and the s in “measure”, again with the tongue curled. Sh and r are a pair: the same tongue position, with r voiced.

rows: like j in “judge”, tongue curled: no puff
like ch in “church”, tongue curled: strong puff

explanations.title: Curled against flat
explanations.body: The sounds in each row below are close for an English ear, but the tongue is in a different place. All the words in this table are tone 4, so only the initial changes.

tables.title: Three places, three kinds
tables.note: Rows: tongue tip down behind the lower teeth, curled back, and behind the upper teeth.

exercises.prompt: Which four initials are made with the tongue curled back?
exercises.explanation: The curled-back group is zh, ch, sh and r.

exercises.prompt: Which of zh, ch and sh has a strong puff?

exercises.explanation: 这 is read zhè and means “this”.
吃 is read chī and means “to eat”.
是 is read shì and means “to be”.
热 is read rè and means “hot”.
书 is read shū and means “a book”.
茶 is read chá and means “tea”.

exercises.prompt: Which is the zh member of the row “zhi, chi, shi” in tone 4?
exercises.explanation: Zh is the curled-back sound without a puff, written zhi.

exercises.prompt: Which pair has the tongue tip down, against the back of the lower teeth?
exercises.explanation: J, q and x keep the tip down. The curled-back and the teeth sounds do not.

lessons.title: 8. The i rule and the u rule
lessons.subtitle: One letter, more than one sound

explanations.title: Three sounds for i
explanations.body: The letter i is not always “ee”. After the curled-back initials zh, ch, sh and r it is a buzz made with the tongue curled, a little like an r. After z, c and s it is a buzz at the teeth. After every other initial it is “ee”, as in “see”. Nothing in the spelling tells you, so the rule is by initial.

explanations.title: Two sounds for u
explanations.body: The letter u is also read two ways. After j, q, x and y it is ü: lips rounded as for “oo”, but with your tongue where it is for “ee”. After any other initial it is “oo”, as in “moon”.

exercises.prompt: How is the i in chī pronounced?
exercises.explanation: After zh, ch, sh and r the i is a buzz made with the tongue curled back.

exercises.prompt: How is the i in jī pronounced?
options: As a buzz at the teeth
exercises.explanation: After j, q, x and most other initials, i is “ee”.

exercises.prompt: How is the i in cì pronounced?
options: As a buzz at the teeth
exercises.explanation: After z, c and s the i is a buzz at the teeth.

exercises.prompt: How is the u in qù pronounced?
exercises.explanation: After j, q, x and y, u stands for ü.

exercises.prompt: How is the u in shū pronounced?
exercises.explanation: After sh, as after most initials, u is “oo”.

exercises.prompt: In which syllable is the i a buzz?
exercises.explanation: After sh the i is a buzz. The others have “ee”.

exercises.prompt: In which syllable is the i NOT a buzz?
exercises.explanation: After n the i is “ee”. The others follow z, ch and r.

exercises.prompt: In which syllable does the u stand for ü?
exercises.explanation: After x the written u is ü.

exercises.prompt: In which syllable is the u an ordinary “oo”?
exercises.explanation: Zh is not one of j, q, x, y, so u is “oo”.
四 is read sì and means “four”.
是 is read shì and means “to be”.
鱼 is read yú and means “fish”.

units.title: 拼音 Pinyin: finals, spelling and tones

lessons.title: 9. The six simple finals
lessons.subtitle: a, o, e, i, u and ü

explanations.title: Six single vowels
explanations.body: Mandarin has six simple finals. A, i, u and ü are close to vowels you already know. O is rounded, and in b, p, m, f syllables you hear a little w before it. E is a relaxed “uh”, said with the lips unrounded. Ü is the odd one for English speakers: say “ee” and, without moving your tongue, round your lips.

tables.note: Remember the i rule (after zh, ch, sh, r, z, c and s it is a buzz) and the u rule (after j, q, x and y it is ü).

explanations.title: The letter e changes with its neighbours
explanations.body: On its own, e is the relaxed “uh”. In ie and üe it is a bright “eh”, as in “let”. In ei it is part of an “ay” sound. These come back in the compound finals.

examples.text: 喝
examples.translation: hē — to drink

examples.text: 写
examples.translation: xiě — to write

examples.text: 月
examples.translation: yuè — moon, month

exercises.prompt: How many simple finals does Mandarin have?
exercises.explanation: The simple finals are a, o, e, i, u and ü.

exercises.prompt: Which simple final is said by rounding your lips while saying “ee”?
Which simple final is a relaxed “uh”?
exercises.explanation: E is a relaxed “uh”, with unrounded lips.

exercises.prompt: The a in mǎ sounds like…

exercises.explanation: 马 is read mǎ and means “a horse”.
波 is read bō and means “a wave”.
喝 is read hē and means “to drink”.
米 is read mǐ and means “rice”.
书 is read shū and means “a book”.
女 is read nǚ and means “woman”.
In ie and üe the e is “eh”.

lessons.title: 10. ai, ei, ao, ou
lessons.subtitle: Four finals that glide

explanations.title: Two vowels, one glide
explanations.body: These four finals start on one vowel and slide toward another, all inside a single syllable. Ai is “eye”. Ei is “ay” as in “day”. Ao is “ow” as in “cow”. Ou is “oh” as in “go”. Say them smoothly: do not stop between the two vowels.

explanations.title: Hearing the difference
explanations.body: Each pair below differs only in the final. Say each aloud and notice where your mouth ends up.

tables.title: ai and ei; ao and ou

exercises.explanation: 来 is read lái and means “to come”.
买 is read mǎi and means “to buy”.
美 is read měi and means “beautiful”.
好 is read hǎo and means “good”.
头 is read tóu and means “a head”.
黑 is read hēi and means “black”.

lessons.title: 11. an, en, ang, eng, ong
lessons.subtitle: n finals and ng finals

explanations.title: Ending on n, ending on ng
explanations.body: Five finals end on a nasal sound. With n at the end, the tip of the tongue goes to the ridge behind the top teeth. With ng, the back of the tongue lifts and the tip stays down, as in English “sing”. An is “ahn”, en is a short “un” (as in “taken”), ang is “ahng”, eng is “ung” and ong is like “oong”, with rounded lips.

explanations.title: Pairs: n against ng
explanations.body: These pairs differ only in the last sound. Say the n ones with the tongue tip up, and the ng ones with the tip down.

exercises.prompt: In which final does the back of the tongue lift, as in “sing”?
exercises.explanation: Ang, eng and ong end in ng.

exercises.prompt: In which final does the tongue tip go to the ridge at the end?
exercises.explanation: An and en end in n.
看 is read kàn and means “to look”.
很 is read hěn and means “very”.
忙 is read máng and means “busy”.
能 is read néng and means “can”.
中 is read zhōng and means “middle”.
帮 is read bāng and means “to help”.

exercises.prompt: Which pair differs only by n against ng?
exercises.explanation: Shen and sheng: the same except for the ng ending.

lessons.title: 12. Finals that start with i
lessons.subtitle: ia, ie, iao, iu, ian, in, iang, ing, iong

explanations.title: A y-glide at the start
explanations.body: Nine finals begin with a quick “ee” that slides into the next sound, a bit like English y. Ia is “yah”, ie is “yeh”, iao is “yow” and iu is “yo”. Ian is not “yan”: it sounds like “yen”. In is “een”, iang is “yahng”, ing is “eeng” and iong is “yoong”.

tables.note: The iu final is really iou, written iu after an initial. A later lesson explains the spelling.

explanations.title: Pairs: in against ing, ian against iang
explanations.body: Again the difference is n or ng at the end.

exercises.explanation: 家 is read jiā and means “home”.
写 is read xiě and means “to write”.
小 is read xiǎo and means “small”.
六 is read liù and means “six”.
天 is read tiān and means “sky, day”.
听 is read tīng and means “to listen”.
想 is read xiǎng and means “to want, to think”.

exercises.prompt: Which pair differs only by n against ng?
exercises.explanation: Jin and jing: the same except for the ng ending.

lessons.title: 13. Finals that start with u or ü, and er
lessons.subtitle: ua, uo, uai, ui, uan, un, uang, üe, üan, ün, er

explanations.title: A w-glide, and the ü finals
explanations.body: Finals that start with u begin with a quick “oo” that slides into the next sound, like English w: ua is “wah”, uo is “wo”, uai is “why”, ui is “way”, uan is “wahn”, un is “wun” (as in “won”) and uang is “wahng”. The ü finals keep the rounded “ee” and add a sound after it: üe is “ü-eh”, üan is “ü-en” and ün is ü plus n.

tables.note: Ui is really uei and un is really uen: those spellings are shortened after an initial. After j, q, x and y the ü loses its dots, so xue, yuan and yun are written as shown.

explanations.title: The er final
explanations.body: Er is the one final that is a whole syllable by itself. Curl your tongue back as you say it: it is close to the American “are”. It also appears at the end of some words as a suffix, but that comes later.

exercises.explanation: 花 is read huā and means “a flower”.
多 is read duō and means “many”.
快 is read kuài and means “fast”.
对 is read duì and means “correct”.
关 is read guān and means “to close”.
床 is read chuáng and means “a bed”.
学 is read xué and means “to study”.
云 is read yún and means “a cloud”.
二 is read èr and means “two”.

exercises.prompt: Which pair differs only by n against ng?
exercises.explanation: Guan and guang: the same except for the ng ending.

lessons.title: 14. Spelling rules
lessons.subtitle: y and w, the missing dots, iu ui un, and the dividing mark

explanations.title: Starting without an initial: y and w
explanations.body: A syllable cannot begin with a bare i, u or ü. When a final that starts with i has no initial, the i is spelled y (or the syllable gets a y in front of it): i becomes yi, ia becomes ya. When a final that starts with u has no initial, the u is spelled w: u becomes wu, ua becomes wa. For ü finals, y is added and the dots are dropped: ü becomes yu, üe becomes yue.

rows: wáng a king; the surname Wang
tables.title: Finals that start with u

explanations.title: Shortened finals, missing dots, and the dividing mark
explanations.body: After an initial, iou, uei and uen are written shorter: iu, ui, un. So l + iou is liu, d + uei is dui and g + uen is gun. After j, q and x the ü is written u, with no dots, because j, q and x can never be followed by a real u: jun, quan, xue. After n and l the dots stay, because nu and nü are different: nǚ, lǜ. Finally, when a syllable starting with a, o or e follows another syllable, an apostrophe marks the break, so that Xī'ān (the city) is not confused with xiān (first).

explanations.title: The dividing mark
explanations.body: Compare these pairs. Without the apostrophe you could not tell where the first syllable ends.

examples.text: 西安
examples.translation: Xī'ān — Xi'an, a city

examples.text: 先
examples.translation: xiān — first

exercises.prompt: How is the final ia written when there is no initial?
exercises.explanation: A bare i becomes y: ia is written ya.

exercises.prompt: How is the final uo written when there is no initial?
exercises.explanation: A bare u becomes w: uo is written wo.

exercises.prompt: How is the final ü written when there is no initial?
exercises.explanation: Ü is written yu, with no dots.

exercises.prompt: How is the final i written when there is no initial?
exercises.explanation: I on its own is written yi.
After an initial, iou is shortened to iu.
After an initial, uei is shortened to ui.
After an initial, uen is shortened to un.
After j, q and x the dots of ü are dropped.
After n and l the dots stay, because nu is a different syllable.

exercises.prompt: In which syllable is the u really ü?
exercises.explanation: After x the written u is ü.

exercises.prompt: How do you tell xī'ān (the city) from xiān (first) in writing?
exercises.explanation: The dividing mark shows where the syllables break.
五 is read wǔ and means “five”.
有 is read yǒu and means “to have”.
月 is read yuè and means “the moon, a month”.

lessons.title: 15. The four tones
lessons.subtitle: High, rising, low and falling

explanations.title: Pitch changes the word
explanations.body: In Mandarin the pitch of a syllable is part of the word. The same letters in a different tone are a different word. There are four tones and a neutral tone. Think of your voice sliding along a line from low to high: the 1st tone stays high and level, the 2nd rises (like “what?”), the 3rd dips low, and the 4th falls sharply (like a firm “No!”).

explanations.title: More sets of four
explanations.body: Practise each set aloud. Keep the vowel the same and move only the pitch.

exercises.prompt: Which tone stays high and level?
exercises.explanation: The 1st tone is high and level.
The 3rd tone is low and dipping.

exercises.prompt: Which tone falls sharply, like a firm “No!”
exercises.explanation: The 4th tone is a sharp fall.

exercises.prompt: Which tone mark is written on mǎ?
exercises.explanation: The 3rd tone mark is a small v-shaped caron.

exercises.prompt: Which tone mark is written on mà?
exercises.explanation: The 4th tone mark falls from left to right.
妈 is read mā and means “mum”.
麻 is read má and means “hemp”.
马 is read mǎ and means “a horse”.
骂 is read mà and means “to scold”.
糖 is read táng and means “sugar”.
树 is read shù and means “a tree”.

exercises.prompt: What does the tone of a syllable do?
options: Nothing, if the letters are the same
It changes only how loud it is
It changes which word it is
exercises.explanation: Same letters, different tone: different word.

lessons.title: 16. Where the tone mark goes
lessons.subtitle: Which vowel carries it

explanations.title: Four rules
explanations.body: The tone mark sits above a vowel. If the syllable has an a, the a gets it. If there is no a, an o or an e gets it. In iu and ui, the mark goes on the second vowel. A single vowel just takes it, and the i loses its dot when it does. In practice the mark goes on the vowel you would stress if you sang the syllable.

exercises.prompt: In hǎo, which letter carries the tone mark?
exercises.explanation: If there is an a, the a gets the mark.

exercises.prompt: In wǒ, which letter carries the tone mark?
exercises.explanation: With no a, the o (or e) gets it.

exercises.prompt: In xué, which letter carries the tone mark?
exercises.explanation: With no a or o, the e gets it.

exercises.prompt: In liù, which letter carries the tone mark?
exercises.explanation: In iu the mark goes on the second vowel.

exercises.prompt: In duì, which letter carries the tone mark?
exercises.explanation: In ui the mark goes on the second vowel.

exercises.prompt: In zǒu, which letter carries the tone mark?
exercises.explanation: In ou the mark goes on the o.

exercises.prompt: What happens to the dot of i in nǐ?
options: Nothing: no tone mark is written
It stays, with the tone mark beside it
exercises.explanation: A tone mark on i takes the place of the dot.
The 3rd tone mark goes on the a: hǎo.
The 4th tone mark goes on the u: liù.
The 4th tone mark goes on the i: duì.
The first syllable has the 4th tone (xiè), and the second is neutral, so it has no mark.

exercises.prompt: Which is nǐ hǎo written correctly?
exercises.explanation: Both syllables are written with the 3rd tone: nǐ hǎo. (How you say it is a different matter: see the lesson on third-tone changes.)

lessons.title: 17. The neutral tone
lessons.subtitle: Light and short, with no mark

explanations.title: A syllable with no tone of its own
explanations.body: Some syllables, mostly the second one in a word, are said lightly and quickly. This is the neutral tone, and it has no tone mark. Say the syllable before it a little louder and let the neutral one fall away. Its pitch depends on the tone before it: it is mid after the 1st and 2nd tones, higher after the 3rd, and low after the 4th.

explanations.title: Where you meet it
explanations.body: Many common words end with a neutral syllable: the suffix 子, the particles 吗, 的 and 了, and doubled family words. A few pairs differ only in whether the second syllable is neutral.

rows: turns a statement into a yes/no question
links a describing word to a noun
marks a change or a completed action
tables.title: Particles

exercises.prompt: How is the neutral tone written in pinyin?
options: With a dot above the vowel
exercises.explanation: The neutral tone has no mark at all.

exercises.prompt: How is the neutral tone said?
exercises.explanation: It is quick and light, with no pitch of its own.

exercises.prompt: Which of these has a neutral-tone syllable?
exercises.explanation: The second syllable of bàba is neutral.

exercises.prompt: Which word is written with a neutral second syllable?
exercises.explanation: Péngyou: the second syllable is neutral, so it has no mark.

exercises.prompt: How do you read 爸爸?
exercises.explanation: 爸爸 is read bàba and means “dad”.

exercises.prompt: How do you read 朋友?
exercises.explanation: 朋友 is read péngyou and means “a friend”.

exercises.prompt: How do you read 你们?
exercises.explanation: 你们 is read nǐmen and means “you (plural)”.

exercises.prompt: How do you read 椅子?
exercises.explanation: 椅子 is read yǐzi and means “a chair”.

exercises.prompt: How do you read 什么?
exercises.explanation: 什么 is read shénme and means “what”.

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between dōngxi and dōngxī?
options: Only the pitch of the first syllable
The first means “a thing”, the second “east and west”
The first is a place, the second a person
exercises.explanation: Only the second syllable changes, and it changes the word: neutral for “thing”, 1st tone for “east and west”.

exercises.prompt: Which particle turns a statement into a yes/no question?
exercises.explanation: 吗 (ma) at the end of a sentence makes it a yes/no question.

lessons.title: 18. Third-tone changes
lessons.subtitle: Two 3rds in a row, and the half-third

explanations.title: Two 3rd tones in a row
explanations.body: The full 3rd tone, low and then rising, is only heard when a syllable is said alone or at the end of a phrase. When two 3rd tones come together, the first becomes a 2nd tone. So 你好 is written nǐ hǎo but said ní hǎo. The change is only in speech. In pinyin both syllables keep their 3rd-tone marks.

explanations.title: The half-third
explanations.body: Before a 1st, 2nd, 4th or neutral tone, the 3rd tone does not rise. You say only the low start, the “half-third”, and the next syllable goes on from there. Again the mark stays the 3rd tone in writing.

exercises.explanation: Two 3rd tones: the first becomes a 2nd tone when you say it.
The first of two 3rd tones becomes a 2nd tone.

exercises.prompt: How is 语法 written in pinyin?
exercises.explanation: Pinyin keeps the 3rd-tone marks, although the first is said as a 2nd tone.

exercises.prompt: How is 你好 written in pinyin?
exercises.explanation: Written nǐ hǎo, said ní hǎo.

exercises.prompt: When is the full dipping-and-rising 3rd tone heard?
options: When the syllable is alone or at the end of a phrase
exercises.explanation: Before another syllable it is shortened or changed.

exercises.prompt: What happens to a 3rd tone before a 4th tone, as in 请问?
exercises.explanation: Only two 3rds in a row trigger the change to a 2nd tone.

exercises.prompt: Which word has two 3rd tones in a row?
exercises.explanation: 水果 is shuǐ-guǒ: both are 3rd tone. 老师 is 3rd then 1st, 请问 3rd then 4th, 旅游 3rd then 2nd.

exercises.prompt: Which word is said with a half-third at the start?
exercises.explanation: 老师 is 3rd then 1st: the 3rd is the half-third.

exercises.prompt: In 你们 (nǐmen), what kind of syllable follows the 3rd tone?
In pinyin, can you write ní hǎo for 你好?
options: Yes: that is the standard spelling
No: it is written with both 3rd-tone marks
exercises.explanation: Pinyin spells the underlying tones. The pronunciation changes in speech.

lessons.title: 19. Reading pinyin
lessons.subtitle: Whole words, with what you have learned

explanations.title: Putting it together
explanations.body: You now have every piece: initials, finals, spelling rules and tones. These are common two-syllable words. Read each aloud, applying the third-tone change and the neutral tone where they apply.

exercises.prompt: How do you read 中国?
exercises.explanation: 中国 is read Zhōngguó and means “China”.

exercises.prompt: How do you read 汉语?
exercises.explanation: 汉语 is read Hànyǔ and means “the Chinese language”.

exercises.prompt: How do you read 北京?
exercises.explanation: 北京 is read Běijīng and means “Beijing”.

exercises.prompt: How do you read 学生?
exercises.explanation: 学生 is read xuésheng and means “a student”.

exercises.prompt: How is 对不起 written in pinyin?
exercises.explanation: Duìbuqǐ: in this word 不 is neutral, so it has no mark.

exercises.prompt: In méiguānxi, which syllable is neutral?
exercises.explanation: 没关系 is méi guān xi: only the last syllable is neutral.

exercises.prompt: In xuésheng, what is the final of the second syllable?

units.title: 第一课 First words and greetings

lessons.title: 20. Numbers 0 to 10
lessons.subtitle: 零 一 二 三 四 五 六 七 八 九 十

explanations.title: Eleven words to count with
explanations.body: Chinese numbers are regular. You will use these every day, and they are good practice for tones. Zero is líng. Numbers above ten are built from these: eleven is “ten-one”, twenty is “two-ten”. In phone numbers and on the radio, 1 is often said yāo instead of yī, so it cannot be mistaken for 7.

explanations.title: Reading digits
explanations.body: To read a string of digits, say each one in turn. This is how you give a number such as a room or a phone number.

examples.text: 一二三四
examples.translation: yī èr sān sì — 1234

examples.text: 五六七八
examples.translation: wǔ liù qī bā — 5678

examples.text: 九零一零
examples.translation: jiǔ líng yī líng — 9010

exercises.explanation: 三 (sān) is three: three horizontal strokes.
二 is read èr and means “2”.
七 is read qī and means “7”.
九 is read jiǔ and means “9”.

exercises.prompt: How do you say 一二三四?
exercises.explanation: Read each digit in turn: yī èr sān sì.

exercises.prompt: How do you say 五六七八?
Why is 1 sometimes said yāo in phone numbers?
options: It is not: that is a mistake
So it is not mistaken for 7
exercises.explanation: On the radio and phone, yāo and qī are more distinct than yī and qī.

lessons.title: 21. Greetings and class
lessons.subtitle: 早, 你好, 谢谢, 再见

explanations.title: Hello, thanks and goodbye
explanations.body: These are the first things you say in a Chinese classroom. 早 means “early” and is how you say good morning. 你好 is the general hello, and 你们好 is hello to more than one person. When you speak to a teacher, add 老师. The word 不 changes to the 2nd tone before a 4th tone, so 不客气 is said búkèqi and written that way.

explanations.title: Class begins and ends
explanations.body: The teacher opens and closes class with these words, and students answer.

exercises.explanation: 不客气 (bú kèqi) means “you are welcome”.
请坐 (qǐng zuò) means “please sit down”.
明天见 (míngtiān jiàn) means “see you tomorrow”.

exercises.prompt: What does 周末快乐 mean?
exercises.explanation: 周末快乐 (zhōumò kuàilè) means “have a good weekend”.

exercises.prompt: What do you say to your teacher when you meet in the morning?
exercises.explanation: 老师早 (lǎoshī zǎo): good morning, teacher.

exercises.prompt: What do you say to several people when you arrive?
exercises.explanation: 你们好 is hello to a group. 你好 is for one person.
Someone says thank you: you answer 不客气, you are welcome.
exercises.promptTranslation: A: Thank you! B: You are welcome!

exercises.explanation: At the end of class the teacher says 再见, goodbye.
exercises.promptTranslation: Class is over. The teacher says: “Goodbye!”

exercises.prompt: How do you say 不客气?
exercises.explanation: 不 becomes 2nd tone before a 4th tone: bú kèqi.
周末 is weekend and 快乐 is happy.

lessons.title: 22. Classroom questions
lessons.subtitle: 有问题吗？ 听懂了吗？

explanations.title: Asking and answering in class
explanations.body: To ask whether someone has a question, add 吗 to the end of a statement: 有问题吗? The answer is just the verb: 有 (I do) or 没有 (I do not). To ask whether someone understood what they heard, say 听懂了吗? and answer 听懂了 or 没听懂. If you did not catch something, you can ask 请你再说一遍, please say it again.

explanations.title: How 吗 works
explanations.body: 吗 turns a statement into a yes/no question without changing the word order. Compare the two lines.

examples.text: 你有问题。
examples.translation: nǐ yǒu wèntí — You have a question.

examples.text: 你有问题吗？
examples.translation: nǐ yǒu wèntí ma — Do you have a question?

exercises.prompt: What does 有问题吗 mean?
exercises.explanation: 有问题吗 (yǒu wèntí ma) means “any questions?”.
没有 (méiyǒu) means “no, I have none”.
没听懂 (méi tīngdǒng) means “I did not understand”.

exercises.prompt: What does 请你再说一遍 mean?
exercises.explanation: 请你再说一遍 (qǐng nǐ zài shuō yíbiàn) means “please say it again”.

exercises.prompt: You did not understand what the teacher said. You say…
exercises.explanation: 没听懂: I did not understand.

exercises.prompt: You want the teacher to repeat. You say…
exercises.explanation: 请你再说一遍: please say it again.

exercises.prompt: The teacher asks 有问题吗？ and you have none. You say…
exercises.explanation: 没有: I do not have any.

exercises.prompt: The teacher asks 有问题吗？ and you do have a question. You say…
What does 吗 do at the end of a sentence?

exercises.explanation: 吗 at the end makes it a yes/no question.
exercises.promptTranslation: Did you understand?

exercises.prompt: How is 有问题吗 written in pinyin?
exercises.explanation: yǒu wèntí ma: ma is neutral and has no mark.

lessons.title: 23. My name is…
lessons.subtitle: 我姓…, 我叫…

explanations.title: I, you, he, she
explanations.body: Chinese pronouns do not change shape. 我 is I or me, 你 is you, 您 is the polite you for one person, and 他 and 她 are he and she, which sound exactly alike. Add 们 to make a plural: 你们, 他们.

explanations.title: Giving your name
explanations.body: A Chinese name puts the family name first. 姓 is for the family name and 叫 is for the whole name or the given name. To ask someone politely for their family name, say 请问，您贵姓? (“May I ask, what is your honourable surname?”). To ask a name casually, say 你叫什么名字?

explanations.title: Putting it together
explanations.body: Read these short exchanges aloud. The names are only examples.

examples.text: 请问，您贵姓？
examples.translation: qǐngwèn, nín guìxìng — May I ask your surname?

examples.text: 我姓张。
examples.translation: wǒ xìng Zhāng — My surname is Zhang.

examples.text: 你叫什么名字？
examples.translation: nǐ jiào shénme míngzi — What is your name?

examples.text: 我叫张华。
examples.translation: wǒ jiào Zhāng Huá — My name is Zhang Hua.

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between 他 and 她 when spoken?
options: 他 is 1st tone and 她 is 3rd
exercises.explanation: 他 and 她 are written differently but sound the same.

exercises.prompt: Which means “you” to be polite to one person?

exercises.explanation: 姓 introduces the family name: 我姓张, my surname is Zhang.
exercises.promptTranslation: My surname is Zhang.

exercises.explanation: 叫 gives your name: 我叫张华.
exercises.promptTranslation: My name is Zhang Hua.

exercises.explanation: 你叫什么名字? is the way to ask “what is your name?”
exercises.promptTranslation: What is your name?

exercises.prompt: Which question asks politely for a family name?
exercises.explanation: 您贵姓 asks for the family name, and is the polite way.

exercises.prompt: In Chinese, which name comes first?
exercises.explanation: Chinese names put the family name first: 张华 is Zhāng (family) Huá (given).

exercises.prompt: How is 我叫张华 said?

lessons.title: 24. Branches of service
lessons.subtitle: 海军, 陆军, 空军, 海军陆战队

explanations.title: Who serves in what
explanations.body: The names of the services are built from the same parts. 军 means military or army. 海 is sea, 陆 is land and 空 is sky, so 海军 is the navy, 陆军 the army and 空军 the air force. 海军陆战队 is the marine corps: “sea-force land-fighting unit”. To say what service you are in, use 是: 我是海军 literally means “I am navy”. Put 美国 in front to say it is the American one.

explanations.title: I am… you are… he is…
explanations.body: The same three sentence patterns work for every service.

examples.text: 我是海军。
examples.translation: wǒ shì hǎijūn — I am in the navy.

examples.text: 你是陆军。
examples.translation: nǐ shì lùjūn — You are in the army.

examples.text: 他是空军。
examples.translation: tā shì kōngjūn — He is in the air force.

examples.text: 她是海军陆战队。
examples.translation: tā shì hǎijūn lùzhànduì — She is in the marine corps.

examples.text: 我是美国陆军。
examples.translation: wǒ shì měiguó lùjūn — I am in the US Army.

exercises.prompt: What does 海军陆战队 mean?
exercises.explanation: 海军陆战队 (hǎijūn lùzhànduì) means “marine corps”.
海 is sea, so 海军 is the navy.
陆 is land, so 陆军 is the army.
空 is sky, so 空军 is the air force.

exercises.prompt: Which character appears in the name of all the services?
How do you say “I am in the army”?
exercises.explanation: 我 is I, 是 is to be, 陆军 is army.

exercises.prompt: What does 你是空军 mean?
options: I am in the air force.
He is in the air force.
You are in the air force.
exercises.explanation: 你 is you and 空军 is air force.
是 links a person to a service: 她是海军陆战队.
exercises.promptTranslation: She is in the marine corps.

exercises.explanation: 美国 in front says it is the United States Navy.
exercises.promptTranslation: I am in the US Navy.

exercises.prompt: Which is the correct pinyin for 海军?
exercises.explanation: Hǎijūn: 3rd tone then 1st tone. The 3rd is a half-third.

lessons.title: 25. Ranks
lessons.subtitle: 少尉, 中尉, 上尉… 少校, 中校, 上校… 少将, 中将, 上将

explanations.title: A pattern you can learn once
explanations.body: Chinese officer ranks are built from two parts. The first part says the grade: 少 (junior), 中 (middle) or 上 (senior). The second says the group: 尉 (company-grade officer), 校 (field-grade officer) or 将 (general officer). Put them together and you get nine ranks. These are also the Chinese names used for the matching US officer ranks.

tables.title: Officer ranks
tables.note: For the US: second lieutenant, first lieutenant, captain; major, lieutenant colonel, colonel; major general, lieutenant general, general. Brigadier general is 准将 zhǔnjiàng.

explanations.title: Other useful words
explanations.body: 兵 is a soldier or private. 军官 is an officer, and 军士 is a non-commissioned officer. 军衔 is a military rank. The Chinese army is called 中国人民解放军, the People's Liberation Army. Ranks and their names change over time, so check a current source before relying on any list.

exercises.prompt: In a rank name, which character means “senior”?
exercises.explanation: 上 is the top grade: 上尉, 上校, 上将.

exercises.prompt: In a rank name, which character means “junior”?
exercises.explanation: 少 is the lowest grade: 少尉, 少校, 少将.

exercises.prompt: Which part of the name says it is a general officer?
exercises.explanation: 将 marks general officers: 少将, 中将, 上将.

exercises.prompt: Which part of the name says it is a field-grade officer (major to colonel)?
exercises.explanation: 校 marks majors, lieutenant colonels and colonels.

exercises.prompt: Which is the more senior rank?
exercises.explanation: 上 is senior to 中 and 少, and 校 outranks 尉.

exercises.prompt: Which is the more senior rank?
exercises.explanation: 将 outranks 校, and 中将 is above 少将.

exercises.prompt: Why check a current source for ranks?
options: Ranks and their names change over time
exercises.explanation: Armies reorganise their ranks, so names and lists can be out of date.

lessons.title: 26. Review: pronunciation and first words
lessons.subtitle: Sounds, tones, greetings, names and services

explanations.title: What you have covered
explanations.body: Lesson 1 gave you the whole sound system: 21 initials, the finals, the spelling rules and five tones, and the third-tone and neutral-tone patterns. It also gave you your first words: numbers to ten, greetings, class expressions, how to say your name, the services and the ranks. These questions mix it all together.

examples.text: 你好！我叫张华。
examples.translation: nǐ hǎo! wǒ jiào Zhāng Huá — Hello! My name is Zhang Hua.

examples.text: 我是海军。
examples.translation: wǒ shì hǎijūn — I am in the navy.

examples.text: 再见，明天见！
examples.translation: zàijiàn, míngtiān jiàn — Goodbye, see you tomorrow!

exercises.prompt: Which initial is said with a strong puff and the tongue tip down?
exercises.explanation: Q is aspirated and made with the tip down. Ch is curled, c is at the teeth.

exercises.prompt: Which initial sounds like the ds in “buds”?
How is the i in shì pronounced?
options: As a buzz at the teeth
exercises.explanation: After sh the i is a curled buzz.

exercises.prompt: How is ü written after j?
exercises.explanation: After j, q and x the dots are dropped: ju, qu, xu.

exercises.prompt: How is the final ia written with no initial?
Where does the tone mark go in liù?
exercises.explanation: In iu the mark goes on the second vowel.
The 4th tone is a sharp fall.
Two 3rd tones: the first is said as a 2nd tone.

options: A light, short syllable with no mark
exercises.explanation: It is said lightly and has no tone mark.
六 is read liù and means “6”.

exercises.prompt: What do you answer to 谢谢？

exercises.explanation: 叫 gives the whole name: 我叫李明.
exercises.promptTranslation: My name is Li Ming.

exercises.prompt: What does 我是陆军 mean?
What does 有问题吗？ ask?
exercises.explanation: 有问题吗 asks if there are questions.

lessons.title: 27. Nice to meet you
lessons.subtitle: 您好, 请问, 认识, 高兴, 也

explanations.title: Meeting someone politely
explanations.body: When you meet a person for the first time you greet them, perhaps ask a question politely, and say you are glad to meet them. 您 is the polite “you”. 请问 is “may I ask”, and it comes before a question. 认识 means to know a person, so 认识你 is “to know you”, and 高兴 means happy. 很 means “very” and comes before 高兴. 也 means “also” and goes right before the verb or adjective.

explanations.title: A first meeting
explanations.body: Here is how a short first meeting goes. The second speaker echoes the first and adds 也.

examples.text: 您好！
examples.translation: nín hǎo — Hello! (polite)

examples.text: 你好！很高兴认识你。
examples.translation: nǐ hǎo! hěn gāoxìng rènshi nǐ — Hello! Nice to meet you.

examples.text: 我也很高兴认识您。
examples.translation: wǒ yě hěn gāoxìng rènshi nín — I am glad to meet you too.

examples.text: 请问，您是王老师吗？
examples.translation: qǐngwèn, nín shì Wáng lǎoshī ma — Excuse me, are you Teacher Wang?

exercises.prompt: What does 很高兴认识你 mean?
exercises.explanation: 很高兴认识你 (hěn gāoxìng rènshi nǐ) means “nice to meet you”.

exercises.prompt: How do you read 认识?
How do you read 高兴?
The other person says 很高兴认识你. A good reply is…
exercises.explanation: Echo the sentence and add 也: 我也很高兴认识你.

exercises.prompt: Which greeting is polite, for someone older or senior?

exercises.explanation: 认识 means to know a person: 很高兴认识你.
exercises.promptTranslation: Nice to meet you.

exercises.explanation: 也 means “also”: 我也很高兴认识你, I am glad to meet you too.
exercises.promptTranslation: I am glad to meet you too.

exercises.explanation: 是 links 您 with 王老师.
exercises.promptTranslation: Excuse me, are you Teacher Wang?

exercises.prompt: Where does 也 go in a sentence?
options: Right before the verb or adjective
exercises.explanation: 也 comes before what it describes: 我也很高兴.

lessons.title: 28. Word order and 什么
lessons.subtitle: 我姓李 · 你姓什么？

explanations.title: Same order for statements and questions
explanations.body: A basic Chinese sentence is Subject + Verb + Object, or Subject + Adjective. A question keeps the very same order. Where English moves words around (“You are called… / What are you called?”), Chinese simply puts the question word in the place where the answer will go. 什么 means “what”, so 你姓什么 asks “you are surnamed what?”

explanations.title: Question and answer share a shape
explanations.body: Compare each question with its answer: only the last part changes.

examples.text: 你姓什么？
examples.translation: nǐ xìng shénme — What is your surname?

examples.text: 我姓李。
examples.translation: wǒ xìng Lǐ — My surname is Li.

examples.text: 你叫什么名字？
examples.translation: nǐ jiào shénme míngzi — What is your name?

examples.text: 我叫李明。
examples.translation: wǒ jiào Lǐ Míng — My name is Li Ming.

examples.text: 王老师叫什么名字？
examples.translation: Wáng lǎoshī jiào shénme míngzi — What is Teacher Wang's name?

exercises.prompt: In a Chinese question, where does 什么 go?
options: At the start of the sentence
exercises.explanation: 什么 takes the place of the answer.

exercises.prompt: Does the word order change when a statement becomes a question with 什么?
options: Yes: 什么 moves to the front
Yes: the verb moves to the front
Yes: the subject moves to the end
exercises.explanation: The order stays the same: 你姓李 becomes 你姓什么.

exercises.prompt: How do you ask “What is your name?”
In 我姓李, which word is the verb?
exercises.explanation: 姓 is the verb: I am surnamed Li.

exercises.prompt: In 他是老师, which word is the object?
exercises.explanation: 老师 comes after the verb 是, so it is the object.
Answer with the same shape: 我姓张.

exercises.prompt: Which answers 你叫什么名字？

exercises.explanation: 什么 asks for the surname.
exercises.promptTranslation: What is your surname?

exercises.explanation: 你叫什么名字 and 王老师叫什么名字 use the same pattern.
exercises.promptTranslation: What is Teacher Wang's name?

exercises.explanation: 叫 goes with the whole name: 我叫李明.
exercises.promptTranslation: My name is Li Ming.

exercises.explanation: 是 links 他 and 老师.
exercises.promptTranslation: He is a teacher.

exercises.prompt: How do you read 什么?

exercises.explanation: 姓 is read xìng and means “to have the surname”.

lessons.title: 29. Yes/no questions with 吗
lessons.subtitle: 你是学生吗？ 是。 不是。

explanations.title: Add 吗 to the end
explanations.body: To ask a yes/no question, take any statement and put 吗 on the end. Nothing else moves. 吗 is a light particle: it is in the neutral tone, and it has no meaning of its own beyond making the sentence a question.

explanations.title: Answering
explanations.body: The answer is the verb of the question: 是 for “yes” and 不是 for “no”. With another verb, repeat that verb: 姓 or 不姓. You can also say 对, “right”, for yes. But for no you do not say 不对, which means “wrong”: you use 不是 or 不.

examples.text: 你是老师吗？ 是。
examples.translation: nǐ shì lǎoshī ma? shì — Are you a teacher? Yes.

examples.text: 你是海军吗？ 不是，我是陆军。
examples.translation: nǐ shì hǎijūn ma? búshì, wǒ shì lùjūn — Are you in the navy? No, I am in the army.

examples.text: 你姓王吗？ 姓。
examples.translation: nǐ xìng Wáng ma? xìng — Is your surname Wang? Yes.

exercises.prompt: How do you turn 你是学生 into a question?
options: Add 什么 at the end

exercises.prompt: What does 你是海军吗？ ask?
What does 他是老师吗？ ask?
exercises.explanation: 他 is he, and 吗 makes it a question.

exercises.prompt: The answer “no” to 你是老师吗？ is…
The answer “yes” to 你姓王吗？ is…
exercises.explanation: Repeat the verb of the question.
对 means right, so it can mean yes. 不对 means wrong.

exercises.promptTranslation: Are you a teacher?
Is your surname Wang?
Is he in the army?

exercises.prompt: A: 你是学生吗？ B: ___，我是学生。
exercises.promptTranslation: Yes, I am a student.

exercises.prompt: A: 你是海军吗？ B: ___，我是空军。
exercises.promptTranslation: No, I am in the air force.

exercises.prompt: Which word turns a statement into a question without changing the word order?
exercises.explanation: 吗 is added at the end.

lessons.title: 30. Saying no with 不
lessons.subtitle: 不是, 不姓, 不好 · bù and bú

explanations.title: 不 goes before the verb or adjective
explanations.body: 不 means “not”. Put it in front of the verb or adjective it negates: 我是老师 becomes 我不是老师. There is no extra word for “do not” or “am not”, only 不.

examples.text: 我不是老师。
examples.translation: wǒ búshì lǎoshī — I am not a teacher.

examples.text: 他不姓王。
examples.translation: tā bú xìng Wáng — His surname is not Wang.

examples.text: 她不是陆军。
examples.translation: tā búshì lùjūn — She is not in the army.

examples.text: 我不高兴。
examples.translation: wǒ bù gāoxìng — I am not happy.

explanations.title: The tone of 不
explanations.body: 不 is bù (4th tone) by itself and before a 1st, 2nd or 3rd tone. Before a 4th tone it becomes bú (2nd tone), because two falling tones in a row are awkward. The pinyin is written with the changed tone, so 不是 is bú shì.

tables.title: bù before tones 1, 2 and 3; bú before 4

options: Right before the verb or adjective
At the end of the sentence
exercises.explanation: 不 goes before what it negates.

exercises.prompt: How do you say “I am not a teacher”?
What does 他不姓王 mean?
What does 她不是陆军 mean?
options: She is not in the army.
He is not in the army.

exercises.prompt: How is 不 pronounced before a 4th tone?
exercises.explanation: Before a 4th tone, 不 is bú, the 2nd tone.

exercises.prompt: How is 不 pronounced in 不好?
exercises.explanation: 好 is the 3rd tone, so 不 keeps the 4th tone.

exercises.prompt: How do you read 不是?
How do you read 不好?
How do you read 不客气?
How do you read 不高兴?

exercises.promptTranslation: I am not a teacher.
His surname is not Wang.

exercises.prompt: 你是学生吗？ 我___是学生。
exercises.promptTranslation: I am not a student.

exercises.prompt: Which is the correct way to write the pinyin of 不对?

lessons.title: 31. And you? 呢
lessons.subtitle: 我姓李，你呢？

explanations.title: A follow-up question
explanations.body: Put 呢 after a noun or a pronoun to ask the same question back. It only works when the question is already clear from what was just said. 我是学生，你呢？ means “I am a student, and you?” The listener knows you are asking whether they are a student.

examples.text: 我姓李，你呢？
examples.translation: wǒ xìng Lǐ, nǐ ne — My surname is Li. And you?

examples.text: 我叫张华，您呢？
examples.translation: wǒ jiào Zhāng Huá, nín ne — My name is Zhang Hua. And you? (polite)

examples.text: 我是学生，你呢？ 我是老师。
examples.translation: wǒ shì xuésheng, nǐ ne? wǒ shì lǎoshī — I am a student. And you? I am a teacher.

examples.text: 我是海军，他呢？ 他是空军。
examples.translation: wǒ shì hǎijūn, tā ne? tā shì kōngjūn — I am in the navy. And he? He is in the air force.

explanations.title: 吗 or 呢?
explanations.body: 吗 turns a whole statement into a yes/no question and can start a conversation. 呢 follows a single noun or pronoun and needs a question already on the table. You cannot open a conversation with 你呢.

rows: I am a teacher. And you? (follow-up)

exercises.prompt: What does 你呢？ mean after 我是学生?
exercises.explanation: 呢 repeats the same question: and are you a student?

options: At the start of a sentence
After a whole statement to make a yes/no question
exercises.explanation: 呢 comes after a noun or pronoun.

exercises.prompt: When can you use 你呢？
options: At the start of a conversation
Only to ask for a name
When the question is already clear from what was said
exercises.explanation: 呢 relies on what came before.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence opens a conversation with a yes/no question?
exercises.explanation: Use 吗 for a new yes/no question.

exercises.prompt: How do you ask politely “And you?” to a teacher?
你姓李吗？ and 我姓李，你呢？ differ because…
options: The second is a follow-up that relies on what was said
exercises.explanation: 吗 asks a new question; 呢 follows up.
你呢 asks for the other person's surname.
exercises.promptTranslation: My surname is Li. And you?
I am in the navy. And he?
My name is Zhang Hua. And you?

exercises.prompt: 我是学生，你___？ 我是老师。
exercises.explanation: 你呢 asks the other person.
exercises.promptTranslation: I am a student. And you?

exercises.prompt: You say 我很高兴认识你. The other person says 我也很高兴认识你. Which word shows “too”?
Which is a correct reply to 我姓赵，你呢？
exercises.explanation: Give your surname: 我姓 + surname.

lessons.title: 32. Who? 谁
lessons.subtitle: 他是谁？ 谁是老师？

explanations.title: 谁 asks about people
explanations.body: 谁 means “who”. The word order is the same as in the answer, so 谁 stands where the person's name or title will be. It can be the object, as in 他是谁 (“he is who”), or the subject, as in 谁是老师 (“who is the teacher”). It is said shuí, and you will also hear it as shéi.

explanations.title: More examples
explanations.body: Notice that the answer takes the place of 谁 and nothing else changes.

examples.text: 你是谁？
examples.translation: nǐ shì shuí — Who are you?

examples.text: 我是李明。
examples.translation: wǒ shì Lǐ Míng — I am Li Ming.

examples.text: 谁是陆军？
examples.translation: shuí shì lùjūn — Who is in the army?

examples.text: 王明是陆军。
examples.translation: Wáng Míng shì lùjūn — Wang Ming is in the army.

exercises.explanation: 是谁 asks who someone is.

exercises.prompt: What does 谁是学生？ ask?
Where is 谁 in the answer?
options: In the same place as the answer

exercises.prompt: Which is the answer to 谁是老师？
Which asks about a name, not about who the person is?
exercises.explanation: 叫什么名字 asks for the name.

exercises.promptTranslation: Who is he?

exercises.explanation: 谁 stands where 王明 stands.
exercises.promptTranslation: Who is in the army?

exercises.explanation: 你是谁 asks who you are.
exercises.promptTranslation: Who are you?

exercises.prompt: 她是___？ 她是我的老师。
exercises.explanation: 她是谁 asks who she is.
exercises.promptTranslation: Who is she?

exercises.prompt: How do you say “Who is the class leader?”
Which question uses 什么, not 谁?
exercises.explanation: 什么 asks about a thing or a word, 谁 about a person.

lessons.title: 33. This and that: 这 and 那
lessons.subtitle: 这是… 那是… 这位 那位

explanations.title: Introducing someone
explanations.body: 这 means “this” and 那 means “that”. To point out a person, use 这是 or 那是 and then the name or title: 这是李明 (“this is Li Ming”). To be more polite you add the measure word 位, which is used for people: 这位是王老师, 那位是谁？

explanations.title: In use
explanations.body: 这 is for the person near you, 那 for the person farther away.

examples.text: 这是李明。
examples.translation: zhè shì Lǐ Míng — This is Li Ming.

examples.text: 那是王老师。
examples.translation: nà shì Wáng lǎoshī — That is Teacher Wang.

examples.text: 这位是谁？
examples.translation: zhèwèi shì shuí — Who is this? (polite)

examples.text: 那位是我们的班长。
examples.translation: nàwèi shì wǒmen de bānzhǎng — That is our class leader.

exercises.explanation: 位 (wèi) means “(polite measure word for people)”.

exercises.prompt: What does 这是李明 mean?
What does 那位是谁？ ask?
Which word makes “this person” more polite?
exercises.explanation: 这位 and 那位 are the polite forms.

exercises.prompt: You are pointing at a person right next to you. You say…
exercises.explanation: 这 is near, 那 is far.

exercises.prompt: You are asking about someone across the room. You say…

exercises.promptTranslation: This is Teacher Wang.
That is our class leader.

exercises.explanation: 位 is the polite measure word for people.
exercises.promptTranslation: Who is this?

exercises.prompt: How do you introduce a person to someone else?

lessons.title: 34. People around you
lessons.subtitle: 同学, 班长, 朋友, 太太, 先生

explanations.title: Classmates, leaders and friends
explanations.body: A 同学 is a classmate, and 班长 is the class leader (the person in charge of a class or squad). 朋友 is a friend: 男朋友 and 女朋友 are boyfriend and girlfriend, because 男 means male and 女 female. 太太 is a wife and 先生 is a husband (it also means “Mr.”). Both 朋友 and 先生 end in a neutral tone.

explanations.title: Introducing people
explanations.body: Use 这是 or 那是 with these words, and 也 and 不 as before.

examples.text: 这是我的同学。
examples.translation: zhè shì wǒ de tóngxué — This is my classmate.

examples.text: 那位是班长，他是海军。
examples.translation: nàwèi shì bānzhǎng, tā shì hǎijūn — That is the class leader; he is in the navy.

examples.text: 她是我的朋友。
examples.translation: tā shì wǒ de péngyou — She is my friend.

examples.text: 他是我太太的老师。
examples.translation: tā shì wǒ tàitai de lǎoshī — He is my wife's teacher.

exercises.prompt: How do you read 同学?
How do you read 朋友?
How do you read 班长?

exercises.explanation: 女 is female: 女朋友 is girlfriend.
男 is male: 男朋友 is boyfriend.

exercises.promptTranslation: This is my classmate.

exercises.explanation: 班长 is the class leader.
exercises.promptTranslation: That is our class leader.

exercises.prompt: How do you say “She is my friend”?
exercises.explanation: 她 is she and 朋友 is friend.

lessons.title: 35. Pronouns, 们 and 的
lessons.subtitle: 我们, 你们, 他们 · 我的, 你的

explanations.title: Pronoun forms
explanations.body: Chinese pronouns do not change for subject and object: 我 is both I and me. Add 们 for the plural, and 的 for the possessive. 他 and 她 sound the same (tā) and differ only in writing. 们 is in the neutral tone, and it is used for people only: 老师们 is fine, but never 房子们.

explanations.title: In pinyin
explanations.body: 您 has no plural of its own: for several people use 你们. 他们 means “they” for men or for a mixed group, and 她们 for women only.

explanations.title: The pattern with 的
explanations.body: Owner + 的 + thing: 我的老师 is “my teacher”.

examples.text: 他是我的老师。
examples.translation: tā shì wǒ de lǎoshī — He is my teacher.

examples.text: 那位是你们的老师吗？
examples.translation: nàwèi shì nǐmen de lǎoshī ma — Is that your (plural) teacher?

examples.text: 我是李明的同学。
examples.translation: wǒ shì Lǐ Míng de tóngxué — I am Li Ming's classmate.

exercises.prompt: How do you read 我们?
How do you read 他们?

exercises.explanation: 们 is the plural marker for people.

exercises.prompt: How is the 们 in 我们 pronounced?
Which word is the polite form of “you”?

exercises.promptTranslation: He is my teacher.
Is that your teacher?
We are all students.

lessons.title: 36. Shortcuts with 的
lessons.subtitle: 我同学, 我太太 · 是我的

explanations.title: Leaving 的 out
explanations.body: With close relations and groups you belong to, 的 is often left out, as in 我同学 and 我太太. You will see the same with family words such as 我爸爸 and 你父母.

explanations.title: Leaving the noun out
explanations.body: When it is clear what the owned thing is, you can drop the noun after 的 and keep 的: 这是你的吗？ 是我的。

examples.text: 这是你的吗？
examples.translation: zhè shì nǐ de ma — Is this yours?

examples.text: 是我的。
examples.translation: shì wǒ de — It is mine.

examples.text: 谁的老师姓王？ 他们的。
examples.translation: shuí de lǎoshī xìng Wáng? tāmen de — Whose teacher is surnamed Wang? Theirs.

examples.text: 李明是谁的同学？ 是我的。
examples.translation: Lǐ Míng shì shuí de tóngxué? shì wǒ de — Whose classmate is Li Ming? Mine.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase leaves 的 out correctly?
exercises.explanation: With close relations, 的 is often dropped.

exercises.prompt: What does 是我的 mean in answer to 这是你的吗？
What does 谁的老师？ ask?
exercises.explanation: 谁的 asks about the owner.

exercises.prompt: Which is a possible answer to 谁的老师姓王？
exercises.explanation: Drop the noun and keep 的: 他们的.

exercises.prompt: Which is a possible answer to 这是你的吗？
exercises.explanation: 不是, 是他的: No, it is his.

exercises.prompt: How do you read 爸爸?
How do you read 妈妈?
How do you read 太太?

exercises.promptTranslation: Is this yours? It is mine.

exercises.prompt: 李明是谁的同学？ 是___。
exercises.promptTranslation: Whose classmate is Li Ming? Mine.
This is my wife.

units.title: 第二课 People, languages and numbers

lessons.title: 37. Adjectives as predicates
lessons.subtitle: 我很好 · 你忙吗？ · 他不高兴

explanations.title: No “to be” with an adjective
explanations.body: In English an adjective needs “am, is, are”: I am happy. In Chinese an adjective works as the predicate by itself, with no 是. You say 我高兴, not 我是高兴. By default, though, an adjective standing alone sounds like a comparison, so there is usually an adverb in front. The usual one is 很, which here is often only a link and does not always mean “very”.

examples.text: 我很高兴。
examples.translation: wǒ hěn gāoxìng — I am happy.

examples.text: 你好吗？ 我很好，谢谢。
examples.translation: nǐ hǎo ma? wǒ hěn hǎo, xièxie — How are you? I am well, thank you.

examples.text: 你忙吗？ 我不忙。
examples.translation: nǐ máng ma? wǒ bù máng — Are you busy? I am not busy.

examples.text: 他也很高兴。
examples.translation: tā yě hěn gāoxìng — He is happy too.

explanations.title: Words to use
explanations.body: These adjectives work in the pattern Subject + (adverb) + adjective. To ask, add 吗; to answer, repeat the adjective.

exercises.explanation: 不错 (búcuò) means “not bad, pretty good”.

exercises.prompt: How do you read 不错?
Do you need 是 before an adjective in Chinese?
exercises.explanation: An adjective is a predicate by itself: 我很高兴.

exercises.prompt: How do you say “I am not busy”?
exercises.explanation: 不 goes before the adjective, with no 是.
好 + 吗: are you well?

exercises.prompt: A good reply to 你高兴吗？ is…

exercises.promptTranslation: I am happy.

exercises.explanation: 吗 turns it into a yes/no question.
exercises.promptTranslation: Are you busy?
I am not busy.
He is happy too.

lessons.title: 38. 很, 也, 都 and 不
lessons.subtitle: 他们都是学生 · 我们也都很好

explanations.title: Adverbs sit before the verb
explanations.body: 很 (very), 也 (also), 都 (both, all) and 不 (not) are adverbs. An adverb always comes before the verb or adjective it describes, never after it. 都 means “both” for two people and “all” for more. When several are present, 也 comes first, then 都, then 很 or 不: 他们也都是学生, 我们都不是老师.

explanations.title: Putting them together
explanations.body: The subject can be one person or many. 都 refers back to the subject, so the subject should be plural.

examples.text: 他也是学生。
examples.translation: tā yě shì xuésheng — He is a student too.

examples.text: 我们都是学生。
examples.translation: wǒmen dōu shì xuésheng — We are all students.

examples.text: 我们都不是老师。
examples.translation: wǒmen dōu búshì lǎoshī — None of us is a teacher.

examples.text: 他们也都很高兴。
examples.translation: tāmen yě dōu hěn gāoxìng — They are all happy too.

examples.text: 我们的中文都很好。
examples.translation: wǒmen de zhōngwén dōu hěn hǎo — Our Chinese is good, all of us.

exercises.explanation: 都 is read dōu when it means “both, all”.

exercises.prompt: Where do adverbs like 也 and 都 go?
options: At the end of the sentence
exercises.explanation: Adverbs come before what they describe.

exercises.prompt: In a sentence with both 也 and 都, which comes first?
exercises.explanation: The order is 也, then 都.

exercises.prompt: What does 我们都是学生 mean?
What does 他们也都很高兴 mean?
What does 我们都不是老师 mean?
options: None of us is a teacher.
exercises.explanation: 都不 means none, or neither.
也 comes before 都, and both before 是.
都 comes before 不: 都不是.

exercises.promptTranslation: We are all students.
He is a student too.
They are all well.
Our Chinese is good.
None of us is a student.

lessons.title: 39. Countries and nationalities
lessons.subtitle: 你是哪国人？ 我是美国人。

explanations.title: Naming countries
explanations.body: 国 means country and 人 means person. A nationality is the country name plus 人: 中国人 is a Chinese person, 美国人 an American. Many foreign country names are written with characters chosen for their sounds, so the characters often do not mean anything on their own.

explanations.title: Which country? 哪国人
explanations.body: 哪 means “which”. 哪国 is “which country”, so 你是哪国人？ asks nationality. It is said nǎ, and many people say něi in 哪国. The answer replaces 哪国: 我是美国人. As always, the word order does not change.

examples.text: 你是哪国人？
examples.translation: nǐ shì nǎ guó rén — What is your nationality?

examples.text: 我是美国人。
examples.translation: wǒ shì Měiguó rén — I am American.

examples.text: 王老师是哪国人？ 他是中国人。
examples.translation: Wáng lǎoshī shì nǎ guó rén? tā shì Zhōngguó rén — What is Teacher Wang's nationality? He is Chinese.

examples.text: 他不是日本人，他是韩国人。
examples.translation: tā búshì Rìběn rén, tā shì Hánguó rén — He is not Japanese; he is Korean.

exercises.prompt: How do you read 美国?
How do you read 韩国?

exercises.explanation: 哪 is which, 国 is country, 人 is person.

exercises.prompt: How do you ask “What is your nationality?”
How do you say “I am Japanese”?

exercises.promptTranslation: What is your nationality?
He is Korean.
I am American.

lessons.title: 40. Languages and departments
lessons.subtitle: 你说中文吗？ 他的韩语很好。

explanations.title: Naming languages
explanations.body: 说 means to speak. A language is the first part of the country's name plus 语 or 文, both of which mean “language”: 中国 gives 中文, 英国 gives 英语 or 英文, 法国 gives 法语 or 法文. The pattern is the same for most languages. 汉语 is also Chinese, and 系 is a university department, as in 中文系.

explanations.title: Speaking and skill
explanations.body: To ask whether someone speaks a language, use 说 and 吗. The answer repeats the verb. To say how good someone's language is, use an adjective with no 是: 他的韩语很好.

examples.text: 你说中文吗？ 说。
examples.translation: nǐ shuō Zhōngwén ma? shuō — Do you speak Chinese? Yes.

examples.text: 他说俄语吗？ 不说。
examples.translation: tā shuō Éyǔ ma? bù shuō — Does he speak Russian? No.

examples.text: 他的韩语很好。
examples.translation: tā de Hányǔ hěn hǎo — His Korean is good.

examples.text: 我的中文不好。
examples.translation: wǒ de Zhōngwén bù hǎo — My Chinese is not good.

examples.text: 她是中文系的老师。
examples.translation: tā shì Zhōngwén xì de lǎoshī — She is a teacher in the Chinese department.

exercises.prompt: How do you read 英语?
What do 语 and 文 mean at the end of 中文 and 英语?
How do you say “Do you speak Chinese?”
A “no” answer to 你说中文吗？ is…
How do you say “His Korean is good”?

exercises.promptTranslation: Do you speak Chinese?
My English is not good.
His Chinese is also good.

lessons.title: 41. Family: parents and spouse
lessons.subtitle: 父亲, 母亲, 父母 · 你父母都是…吗？

explanations.title: Parents
explanations.body: 爸爸 and 妈妈 are dad and mum, and they are what people say at home. 父亲 and 母亲 are the more formal words, father and mother, and 父母 is “parents”. As with other close family, the 的 is usually dropped: 你父母, 我父亲, 她母亲.

explanations.title: Asking about family
explanations.body: Put the family word where the subject is and add 哪国人 or 吗. 都 is natural when you ask about both parents.

examples.text: 你父母都是美国人吗？
examples.translation: nǐ fùmǔ dōu shì Měiguó rén ma — Are your parents both American?

examples.text: 不是，我父亲是美国人，母亲是中国人。
examples.translation: búshì, wǒ fùqīn shì Měiguó rén, mǔqīn shì Zhōngguó rén — No: my father is American and my mother is Chinese.

examples.text: 你太太是哪国人？
examples.translation: nǐ tàitai shì nǎ guó rén — What is your wife's nationality?

examples.text: 她是德国人，她也说中文。
examples.translation: tā shì Déguó rén, tā yě shuō Zhōngwén — She is German; she also speaks Chinese.

exercises.prompt: How do you read 父亲?
How do you read 母亲?
How do you read 父母?
Which are the more formal words for parents?
exercises.explanation: 父亲, 母亲 are father and mother, in formal speech.

exercises.prompt: What does 你父母都是美国人吗？ ask?
What does 我父亲是美国人，母亲是中国人 mean?
options: My father is American and my mother is Chinese.
My mother is American and my father is Chinese.
exercises.explanation: 父亲 is father, 母亲 is mother.

exercises.prompt: How do you ask “What is your wife's nationality?”
我___是美国人，母亲是中国人。 (father)
exercises.promptTranslation: My father is American; my mother is Chinese.
What is your wife's nationality?

lessons.title: 42. Phone numbers
lessons.subtitle: 电话号码, 手机 · 多少？

explanations.title: Asking for a number
explanations.body: 电话 is a telephone, 手机 is a cell phone (“hand machine”), and 号码 is a number. 多少 means “how many” or “how much”, and it is the question word for numbers. The answer replaces 多少 as usual. 对了 is “oh, right”, a handy way to change the subject to the number.

explanations.title: Saying digits
explanations.body: Say each digit in turn, even for a long number. For 1, people usually say yāo instead of yī on the phone and the radio, so that it cannot be mistaken for 7 (qī). The character 幺 is used for 1 when it is read yāo. In military radio use the digits 0, 7 and 9 are said 洞, 拐 and 勾; Lesson 62 teaches them.

examples.text: 你的电话号码是多少？
examples.translation: nǐ de diànhuà hàomǎ shì duōshǎo — What is your phone number?

examples.text: 我的号码是幺三五，二四六八。
examples.translation: wǒ de hàomǎ shì yāo sān wǔ, èr sì liù bā — My number is 135, 2468.

examples.text: 对了，你的手机号码是多少？
examples.translation: duìle, nǐ de shǒujī hàomǎ shì duōshǎo — By the way, what is your cell phone number?

examples.text: 我的手机号码是九零幺七，八六五四。
examples.translation: wǒ de shǒujī hàomǎ shì jiǔ líng yāo qī, bā liù wǔ sì — My cell phone number is 9017 8654.

exercises.explanation: 多少 (duōshǎo) means “how many, how much”.

exercises.prompt: How do you read 电话?
How do you read 手机?
How do you read 号码?
How do you read 多少?
How do you ask “What is your phone number?”
exercises.explanation: 多少 is the question word for numbers.

exercises.prompt: Why is 1 often said yāo in phone numbers?
options: So it is not confused with 7
exercises.explanation: yāo and qī are clearer apart than yī and qī.

exercises.prompt: Which character is read yāo and stands for 1?
How do you say 一三五？ on the phone?
How do you say 九零？
exercises.explanation: 九 is jiǔ and 零 is líng.
多少 asks for a number.
exercises.promptTranslation: What is your phone number?
What is your cell phone number?

exercises.prompt: ___，你的手机号码是多少？ (by the way)
exercises.explanation: 对了 changes the subject politely.
exercises.promptTranslation: By the way, what is your cell phone number?

lessons.title: 43. Chinese names
lessons.subtitle: 姓 and 名 · 王, 李, 张, 刘…

explanations.title: Surname first, given name second
explanations.body: A Chinese name has two parts: the surname (姓) comes first and the given name (名) comes second. Most surnames are one character, like 王, 李 and 张, but a few are two, such as 欧阳 and 司马, which are called compound surnames. Given names are usually one or two characters, so a full name usually has two to four. Women keep their own surname after marriage.

explanations.title: Twenty common surnames
explanations.body: There are only a few hundred common surnames, but countless given names: the opposite of English, where first names repeat and surnames vary. These are among the most common.

explanations.title: Choosing a given name
explanations.body: Parents often choose characters for a good meaning, such as strength, beauty, health or good fortune, or simply a pleasant sound. Boys' names are more likely to use words like 强 (strong) and 伟 (great), and girls' names words for flowers, beauty and gentleness. Some names show the era: after 1949 names like 建军, “build the army”, became common.

examples.text: 他姓王，叫王强。
examples.translation: tā xìng Wáng, jiào Wáng Qiáng — His surname is Wang; he is called Wang Qiang.

examples.text: 她姓欧阳，叫欧阳文。
examples.translation: tā xìng Ōuyáng, jiào Ōuyáng Wén — Her surname is Ouyang; she is called Ouyang Wen.

examples.text: 你好，我姓林，叫林建军。
examples.translation: nǐ hǎo, wǒ xìng Lín, jiào Lín Jiànjūn — Hello, my surname is Lin; I am called Lin Jianjun.

exercises.prompt: In a Chinese name, which part comes first?
What is the surname in 张华？
exercises.explanation: 张 is the surname; 华 is the given name.

exercises.prompt: What is the given name in 李明？
What is the surname in 欧阳文？
exercises.explanation: 欧阳 is a two-character surname.

exercises.prompt: What is the given name in 王小红？
exercises.explanation: 小红 is a two-character given name.

exercises.prompt: What do you call a two-character surname?
exercises.explanation: 欧阳 and 司马 are compound surnames.

exercises.prompt: What does a woman usually do with her surname after marriage?
exercises.explanation: Chinese women keep their original surname.

exercises.prompt: How are surnames and given names usually distributed in Chinese?
options: Few common surnames, countless given names
exercises.explanation: There are few common surnames, but given names are countless.
王 is read Wáng and means “the surname Wang”.
李 is read Lǐ and means “the surname Li”.
张 is read Zhāng and means “the surname Zhang”.
刘 is read Liú and means “the surname Liu”.
陈 is read Chén and means “the surname Chen”.
赵 is read Zhào and means “the surname Zhao”.
孙 is read Sūn and means “the surname Sun”.
高 is read Gāo and means “the surname Gao”.

lessons.title: 44. Aircraft words
lessons.subtitle: 飞机, 直升机, 战斗机, 轰炸机

explanations.title: 机, the machine
explanations.body: 机 means a machine, and it ends most words for aircraft. 飞 is to fly, so 飞机 is “flying machine”, an aeroplane. The name for each type adds a descriptive part in front: 直升 (rising straight up) gives 直升机, a helicopter, and 轰炸 (to bomb) gives 轰炸机, a bomber. You will meet these words in the air force, 空军.

explanations.title: In sentences
explanations.body: These words work like any noun.

examples.text: 他是空军，他的飞机很大。
examples.translation: tā shì kōngjūn, tā de fēijī hěn dà — He is in the air force; his aircraft is big.

examples.text: 这是直升机，那是轰炸机。
examples.translation: zhè shì zhíshēngjī, nà shì hōngzhàjī — This is a helicopter; that is a bomber.

examples.text: 你是陆军，你的直升机也很大吗？
examples.translation: nǐ shì lùjūn, nǐ de zhíshēngjī yě hěn dà ma — You are in the army; is your helicopter big too?

exercises.prompt: How do you read 飞机?
How do you read 直升机?
How do you read 轰炸机?
What does 机 mean on its own?
exercises.explanation: 机 is machine; it ends most aircraft words.

exercises.prompt: Which character ends nearly every word for an aircraft?

exercises.promptTranslation: This is a helicopter; that is a bomber.
He is in the air force; his aircraft is big.

lessons.title: 45. Sound pairs: initials
lessons.subtitle: j q x · z c s · zh ch sh r

explanations.title: j, q, x with ü
explanations.body: After j, q and x the “u” is really ü (the dots are dropped), so jī and jū, qī and qū, xī and xū sound different even though the letters look nearly the same. Say the pairs aloud and listen for the lip rounding in the second word.

tables.title: j q x: i or ü

explanations.title: z, c, s and zh, ch, sh, r
explanations.body: z, c and s are made with the tongue tip flat behind the teeth; zh, ch, sh and r with the tip curled back. z and zh are not puffed, and c and ch are puffed.

exercises.explanation: 鸡 is read jī and means “a chicken”.
居 is read jū and means “to live”.
区 is read qū and means “a region”.
需 is read xū and means “to need”.
七 is read qī and means “seven”.
决 is read jué and means “to decide”.
杂 is read zá and means “mixed”.
擦 is read cā and means “to wipe”.
撒 is read sā and means “to sprinkle”.
在 is read zài and means “at, in”.
村 is read cūn and means “a village”.
这 is read zhè and means “this”.
出 is read chū and means “to go out”.
杀 is read shā and means “to kill”.
肉 is read ròu and means “meat”.
人 is read rén and means “a person”.

exercises.prompt: In which word is the tongue tip flat, behind the teeth?
exercises.explanation: c is made with the tip flat; ch, sh and r are curled.

exercises.prompt: In which word is the tongue tip curled back?
exercises.explanation: sh is curled; s, c and z are flat.

lessons.title: 46. Sound pairs: finals
lessons.subtitle: ua/uo · uo/ou · ie/üe · iao/iu · en/eng · in/ing

explanations.title: Pairs that look alike
explanations.body: Many final pairs differ in a single sound. Listen to what changes: the final glide (ua and uo), the order of the vowels (uo and ou), the lip shape (ie and üe), the ending vowel (iao and iu) and the ending nasal (n and ng).

explanations.title: More pairs
explanations.body: iao and iu: jiào and jiù. en and eng, in and ing: the ending n has the tongue tip up at the end, and ng has it back.

exercises.explanation: 袜 is read wà and means “a sock”.
卧 is read wò and means “to lie down”.
瓜 is read guā and means “a melon”.
锅 is read guō and means “a pot”.
货 is read huò and means “goods”.
偷 is read tōu and means “to steal”.
拖 is read tuō and means “to drag”.
走 is read zǒu and means “to walk”.
左 is read zuǒ and means “left”.
够 is read gòu and means “enough”.
夜 is read yè and means “night”.
月 is read yuè and means “the moon”.
靴 is read xuē and means “boots”.
叫 is read jiào and means “to call”.
旧 is read jiù and means “old”.
秋 is read qiū and means “autumn”.
风 is read fēng and means “wind”.
镇 is read zhèn and means “a town”.
金 is read jīn and means “gold”.
请 is read qǐng and means “please, to invite”.
您 is read nín and means “you (polite)”.

options: 瓜 guā and 锅 guō
夜 yè and 月 yuè
叫 jiào and 旧 jiù
金 jīn and 京 jīng
exercises.explanation: n and ng differ by the ending nasal.
